Separates water faces into two rendering buckets based on Y-coordinate relative to sea level to optimize reflection/refraction passes.
Faces at $Y = \text{seaLevel}$ (default 65) are routed to the ocean bucket, which uses the planar reflection/refraction FBOs.
All other water faces (side faces of sea-level blocks, placed/spread water, deeper top faces) are routed to the placed bucket, which uses a sky-reflection shader independent of global planes.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(N)$ where $N$ is the number of visible fragments, as it requires two full scene renders (reflection and refraction) plus one water surface render.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(W \times H)$ for the two FBOs, where $W, H$ are the resolution of the FBOs.
Refraction resolution is scaled by `refractionResolutionScale`.
However, it is efficient for voxel engines where geometry is highly structured and culling is effective.
The use of clip planes reduces the number of fragments processed in each pass.
*   **Strengths:** Simple implementation, works well for flat water surfaces, provides realistic reflections and refractions for planar water.
Not suitable for complex, non-planar water surfaces.
Precision issues at large world coordinates require UV anchoring.
*   **When to use:** When rendering flat, horizontal water surfaces in a voxel or low-poly environment.
*   **When not to use:** For non-planar water, or when performance is critical and reflections/refractions are not required.
This method is implemented in the `ft_minecraft` voxel engine, a from-scratch project inspired by Minecraft, built as a follow-up to the `ft_vox` project at 42.
The engine emphasizes procedural generation and rendering quality, using OpenGL 4.6 and C++20.
